header.account: A US criminal and traffic defense law firm

executive_summary: September brought 186 leads (the calls and contact forms Google Ads counts, not signed clients; some callers may be counted twice, see the appendix) at a $30 cost per lead: 11% below the June-August average of 209, at a cost per lead 7% higher. The main cause was budget, not ad quality: the two non-brand campaigns that bring in the cheapest leads (Criminal Defense and Traffic Tickets) were capped in early September and lost 41% and 27% of their possible ad views, while Drug Charges spent 55% more at $124 a lead. Budgets on the cheap campaigns were raised on Sep 14 and Sep 28. October priority: keep the money on those two and confirm the budget reset made on Oct 1.

columns_in_plain_words.impression_share: of the searches where the ad could have shown, the share where it did
columns_in_plain_words.lost_to_budget: the share it missed because the daily budget had run out
columns_in_plain_words.lost_to_rank: the share it missed because its ad rank (bid, ad quality and landing page) was too low
columns_in_plain_words.cpa_vs_account: the campaign's cost per lead divided by the account's: below 1.00x is cheaper than average

campaign_performance.tiers_rule: star: CPA at most 0.8x account CPA with 5+ conversions; solid: up to 1.2x; needs attention: above 1.2x, or under 5 conversions on spend of 3x account CPA or more; low volume: the rest

key_insights.observation: Leads (conversions) fell 8% to 186 while spend fell 5%, so the cost per lead (CPA) rose 3% to $30.
key_insights.meaning: Volume, not efficiency, drove the miss: the share of clicks that became a lead improved (25.1% vs 23.4%), but clicks fell 14% and cost per click rose 10%.
key_insights.action: Win back click volume in the campaigns that convert cheapest (next insight) before chasing a lower CPA.

key_insights.observation: The two cheapest non-brand campaigns were held back by budget: Criminal Defense ($21 a lead) missed 41% of the searches where its ad could have shown because its daily budget had run out (impression share lost to budget), and Traffic Tickets ($25 a lead) missed 27%, up from 34% and 5% in August.
key_insights.meaning: The daily budgets in force until Sep 14 were 37% and 35% below what each campaign spent per day in August, and August's spend is more than Google allows in a month on those budgets (30.4 days' worth), so both budgets were cut before Sep 6, outside the change history this report can read. Their spend fell 33% and 21%.
key_insights.action: Keep the Sep 14 and Sep 28 budget raises on these two campaigns, and confirm with the team why they were cut in early September.

key_insights.observation: Drug Charges spent $870 (+55% on August) for 7.0 conversions, a $124 CPA, 4.13x the account average.
key_insights.meaning: It took 16% of spend and returned 4% of conversions. It also ran out of budget (27% of possible ad views lost), but more budget would buy more expensive leads.
key_insights.action: Hold Drug Charges at September's spend or lower, and review its search terms and landing page before adding money.

key_insights.observation: DUI spend rose 63% but it lost 61% of its possible ad views to ad rank (Google's score for each ad, built from the bid, the ad's quality and the landing page) and only 4% to budget; after the Sep 14 budget raise its spend per day fell 55% (Sep 14-27 against Sep 6-13) instead of rising.
key_insights.meaning: Budget isn't what limits DUI: its ads lose auctions because they rank too low.
key_insights.action: Treat DUI as a quality problem, not a budget one. Its target cost per lead was removed on Sep 28, so judge it again in October.

key_insights.observation: Mobile drove 89% of conversions on 93% of spend; desktop cost $21 a lead vs $31 on mobile, on 18.4 conversions.
key_insights.meaning: This is a phone-first account; desktop looks cheaper but on too few conversions to act on yet.
key_insights.action: Watch, don't change: check the desktop CPA again after another month.

items.result: Too early to judge: 3 days of data before month end

Also 1 negative keyword (a search the ads should not show for) added in DUI.

day_and_hour.rule: Flag a weekday or a 6-hour band whose cost per lead is at least 1.3x the account's on at least 10% of spend. One month is a hint, not a reason to change the ad schedule.
day_and_hour.reading: Overnight and evening cost $42 and $40 a lead (1.42x and 1.33x the account's) on 12% and 11% of spend. No weekday is flagged; September had 5 Tuesdays and Wednesdays and 4 of every other day, so compare weekdays per day or by cost per lead, not by totals. Watch these hours in October and check when calls are answered before limiting when the ads run.

appendix.lead_mix_note: 141 of 186 conversions (76%) come from call-type actions in two categories. Check that one caller isn't counted by both before reporting leads as people (the conversion-tracking-auditor skill, if installed).

search_terms.note: Google hides low-volume terms, so these figures cover only the visible share. Term texts are withheld in this sample; the full list goes to search-term-gold-miner.

data_notes: Every number comes from the 12 calls listed in sample_input.json; nothing was typed in.
Leads are the conversions Google Ads counts (calls and contact forms). They aren't signed clients, and two call-type actions may count one caller twice (see the lead mix note).
No goals were given, so conversions and CPA are graded against the Jun-Aug 2026 average and labelled that way.
ROAS isn't reported: September has no conversion value recorded (the last month with any was Jul 2025).
Impression share is per month and per quarter; it can't be added across months.
Change history covers Sep 6 - Oct 5 only (Google keeps 30 days); Sep 1-5 changes are unknown unless the team adds them, so before/after comparisons start on Sep 6.
Campaign spend for September adds up to the account total, and so do the day-and-hour rows.
